outcomes: Describes Black's setup in the main Slav (c6, Nf6, dxc4, Bf5, e6, Bb4, castling) and gives a reason for each piece
Describes White's setup (Nf3, Nc3, a4, e3, Bxc4, castling, Qe2) and says what each move prepares, by imagining the position without it
Explains why the c8 bishop goes out before e6, why a4 comes before e3, and what the pin on c3 forces
Compares two ways of regaining the c4 pawn (Ne5 and e3) and says what each prepares

steps.caption: White to move after eight moves each. Look at Black's pieces one at a time: the pawn on c6, the knight on f6, the bishop on f5, the pawn on e6, the bishop on b4, the king castled. For each, ask what it is doing and which later move it made possible.

claims.statement: Black's king has castled to the kingside.
The bishop on f5 attacks e4, d3 and c2.
The bishop on b4 attacks the knight on c3.

steps.prompt: Before reading on: which one of Black's moves here do you think was the most important to get in early, and what did it make possible?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Every opening move either does something now or makes a later move possible. In the Slav, which move prepares which? We test each idea by taking the move away and watching what breaks. By the end you can describe each side's setup, give a reason for each piece, and say which reasons still hold when the order changes. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference.

steps.caption: White to move after 2...c6. Count the guards and attackers of d5 as the moves go by. Three guards against two attackers means Black is not forced to take on c4: Black may choose when.

line.say: The knight develops and guards d4 and e5.
This knight develops and adds a third guard of d5.
White attacks d5 a second time and prepares e4.
Black takes the pawn. With d5 safe, this is a choice: keep the pawn with ...b5, or give it back for development.

claims.statement: After ...Nf6 three black units guard d5: the c6 pawn, the f6 knight and the queen.
After Nc3 two white units attack d5: the c4 pawn and the c3 knight.
After ...dxc4 a black pawn stands on c4.

steps.caption: Black to move after 5.a4. Remove the first move and see: what if Black plays ...e6 at once? In masters' games from here Black played ...Bf5 in 1,071 games (White won 313, 547 drawn, Black won 211) and ...e6 in 347 (102, 194, 51).

line.say: The bishop leaves c8 while its diagonal is still open.
White opens the diagonal of the f1 bishop, aimed at c4.
Now ...e6 is safe: the bishop is outside the chain and the f8 bishop's diagonal is open.

claims.statement: Before any pawn move the c8 bishop can reach 5 squares.
After ...e6 at once the c8 bishop can reach only d7.
At depth 16 ...e6 at once is at least 0.15 pawn worse than ...Bf5.
After ...e6 the f8 bishop attacks along the diagonal through e7, d6, c5 and b4.

steps.caption: White to move after 4...dxc4. The a4 move is missing here. Masters played 5.a4 in 1,517 games (White won 461, 779 drawn, Black won 277), 5.e4 in 185 (78, 56, 51) and 5.e3 in 22 (10, 11, 1). Is a4 only a habit?

line.say: The natural developing move, but it does not stop what follows.
Black keeps the extra pawn with a pawn.
White attacks the b5 pawn.
Black attacks the knight and the pawn on c4 stays Black's.

claims.statement: After ...b5 one black pawn protects the pawn on c4.
After 5.a4 the engine at depth 16 rates the position between +0.10 and +0.60 for White.
After 5.e3 b5 6.a4 b4 the engine at depth 16 rates the position between -0.40 and +0.40 for White.

steps.caption: Black to move after 7.Bxc4. Masters played 7...Bb4 in 282 games (White won 72, 163 drawn, Black won 47) and ...Nbd7 in 32. Read three moves as a chain: the pin, then both kings castle.

line.say: The bishop pins the knight on c3 to the king.
White castles, which ends the pin.
Black castles too: the king is safe and a rook is free.

claims.statement: After ...Bb4 the knight on c3 has no legal move: it is pinned.
After O-O White's king is on the kingside.
After ...O-O Black's king is on the kingside.

steps.caption: White to move after both kings have castled. Two more links: where the queen goes, and where the f5 bishop goes. Say what each move prepares.

line.say: The queen defends the bishop on c4 and leaves d1 free for a rook.
The bishop steps off f5 before e4 can attack it (the pin is over) and still watches e4. The price: Nh4 can trade it off.

claims.statement: After Qe2 the queen defends the bishop on c4.
After Qe2 the d1 square is empty.
After ...Bg6 the bishop attacks e4.
At depth 16 the final position is rated between -0.10 and +0.80 for White.

steps.text: **Same plan, other order.** A move order changes what the opponent may do, not what the pieces want. [I] Masters' data: the third White move was the f3 knight in 6,638 games and the c3 knight in 1,897. After the knights were out, Black answered with the e-pawn in 2,227 games, took on c4 in 1,742 and played a6 in 998. Next: a choice White faces at move six.

steps.caption: White to move after 5...Bf5. Masters played 6.Ne5 in 615 games (White won 198, 295 drawn, Black won 122) and 6.e3 in 330 (87, 185, 58). Two ways to the same pawn.

line.say: The knight attacks c4 at once, so e3 is not needed first.
Black challenges the centralised knight.
White regains the pawn with the knight.
Black attacks the knight again and gains a tempo.

claims.statement: After Ne5 the knight attacks c4.
After ...Nbd7 the knight attacks e5.
After Nxc4 a white knight stands on c4.
After ...Nb6 the knight attacks c4 and a4.
At depth 16 the final position is rated between 0.00 and +0.80 for White.

steps.caption: A typical mistake for Black, after 7.Bxc4. The move ...b5 looks active, because it hits the bishop. Ask first: what does the a4 pawn attack? (This move is not among the replies listed in our masters data.)

line.say: Black attacks the bishop, hoping to gain a tempo.
White takes: the a-pawn was aimed at b5 all along.
Black recaptures.
The bishop takes the pawn with check. White is a pawn up.
Black blocks the check and develops, but is a pawn down and the pinned knight on d7 is a target.

claims.statement: After ...b5 one white pawn (a4) attacks b5.
At depth 16 ...b5 is at least 1.5 pawns worse than the best move.
At depth 16 the final position is rated between +1.00 and +5.00 for White.

steps.caption: A typical mistake for White, with the pin on. A pawn move to e4 looks like the natural way to claim the centre and hit the f5 bishop. Ask first: which of my pieces can recapture on e4?

line.say: White attacks the bishop with a pawn and hopes to build the centre.
Black takes the pawn, and the pinned knight on c3 cannot take it back.

claims.statement: After e4 the knight on c3 still has no legal move.
The bishop on f5 attacks e4.
After ...Bxe4 a black bishop stands on e4.
At depth 16 the final position is rated between -3.00 and -0.60 for White.

steps.text: **Setup in one view.** Black: the c-pawn guards d5; the g8 knight develops and also guards d5; the d-pawn takes c4; the c8 bishop goes out; the e-pawn closes the centre and opens the f8 bishop, which pins; then castling. White: both knights develop; the a-pawn holds back ...b5; the e-pawn or the f3 knight regains c4; castling ends the pin; the queen and a rook take the centre. [I] Learn the reasons, not the list.

**Recap.**
A move prepares another when the second needs the first.
Bishop out, then ...e6. ...e6 first shuts the c8 bishop in for now; masters did play it (347 games, near-equal results), but then the bishop must be freed another way.
a4 stops ...b5 holding the extra pawn.
The pin on c3 ends with castling; e3 or Ne5 regains c4.
When the order changes, ask which reason still holds.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. A friend asks: why do both sides play these moves in this order? Write the setup for one side, the reason for each move, one move whose order matters, and one mistake a beginner would make. Then check: did you say what each move prepares?
